evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations.

claim: TDP-43 nuclear clearing and foci formation was more robust in hiPSC-derived neurons compared to mouse neurons.
source: We note that TDP-43 nuclear clearing and foci formation was more robust in hiPSC-derived neurons compared to mouse neurons, suggesting human neurons may be more sensitive to TDP-43 RNA-binding deficiency.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparing the experimental results in hiPSC-derived neurons to mouse neurons.

claim: Human neurons may be more sensitive to TDP-43 RNA-binding deficiency than mouse neurons.
source: We note that TDP-43 nuclear clearing and foci formation was more robust in hiPSC-derived neurons compared to mouse neurons, suggesting human neurons may be more sensitive to TDP-43 RNA-binding deficiency.
evidence: This claim is speculated based on the observation that hiPSC-derived neurons show more robust TDP-43 pathology.

claim: hiPSC-derived TDP-43K145R neurons were indistinguishable from TDP-43wt neurons.
source: Similar to mouse neurons, hiPSC-derived TDP-43K145R neurons were indistinguishable from TDP-43wt neurons, supporting acetylation-induced charge neutralization as a driver of TDP-43 loss of function rather than an inherent effect of mutation at the K145 locus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: There was an approximately twofold increase in TARDBP mRNA in TDP-43K145Q.12 and TDP-43K145Q.18 neurons.
source: In contrast to mouse neurons, we observed an approximately twofold increase TARDBP mRNA in TDP-43K145Q.12 and TDP-43K145Q.18 neurons and a slight but significant reduction in TARDBP mRNA in TDP-43K145R.12 neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a slight but significant reduction in TARDBP mRNA in TDP-43K145R.12 neurons.
source: In contrast to mouse neurons, we observed an approximately twofold increase TARDBP mRNA in TDP-43K145Q.12 and TDP-43K145Q.18 neurons and a slight but significant reduction in TARDBP mRNA in TDP-43K145R.12 neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The aberrant SORT1+ex17b splice variant was undetectable in TDP-43wt neurons.
source: The aberrant SORT1+ex17b splice variant was undetectable in TDP-43wt neurons, but was present in 60% of TDP-43K145Q.12 and 100% of TDP-43K145Q.18, TDP-43K145R.2, and TDP-43K145R.12 neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The aberrant SORT1+ex17b splice variant was present in 60% of TDP-43K145Q.12 neurons.
source: The aberrant SORT1+ex17b splice variant was undetectable in TDP-43wt neurons, but was present in 60% of TDP-43K145Q.12 and 100% of TDP-43K145Q.18, TDP-43K145R.2, and TDP-43K145R.12 neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The aberrant SORT1+ex17b splice variant was present in 100% of TDP-43K145Q.18 neurons.
source: The aberrant SORT1+ex17b splice variant was undetectable in TDP-43wt neurons, but was present in 60% of TDP-43K145Q.12 and 100% of TDP-43K145Q.18, TDP-43K145R.2, and TDP-43K145R.12 neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Truncated STMN2 mRNA was approximately 100-fold higher in both TDP-43K145Q.12 and TDP-43K145Q.18 neuron lines compared to TDP-43wt neurons.
source: Strikingly, truncated STMN2 mRNA was approximately 100-fold higher in both TDP-43K145Q.12 and TDP-43K145Q.18 neuron lines, respectively, compared to TDP-43wt neurons, while no difference from WT was found in TDP-43K145R neurons. (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: No difference in truncated STMN2 mRNA from WT was found in TDP-43K145R neurons.
source: Strikingly, truncated STMN2 mRNA was approximately 100-fold higher in both TDP-43K145Q.12 and TDP-43K145Q.18 neuron lines, respectively, compared to TDP-43wt neurons, while no difference from WT was found in TDP-43K145R neurons. (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The unperturbed STMN2 splice variant (STMN2 WT) was reduced about 50% in both acetylation-mimic TDP-43K145Q lines.
source: The unperturbed STMN2 splice variant (STMN2 WT) was reduced about 50% in both acetylation-mimic TDP-43K145Q lines but unchanged in TDP-43K145R.2 neurons (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: STMN2 WT mRNA was unchanged in TDP-43K145R.2 neurons.
source: The unperturbed STMN2 splice variant (STMN2 WT) was reduced about 50% in both acetylation-mimic TDP-43K145Q lines but unchanged in TDP-43K145R.2 neurons (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Both TDP-43K145Q lines dramatically accumulated the UNC13A cryptic exon containing mRNA.
source: In contrast, both TDP-43K145Q lines dramatically accumulated the UNC13A cryptic exon containing mRNA (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Endogenously expressed acetylation-mimic TDP-43K145Q alters TDP-43 localization in response to stress in human iPSC-derived neurons.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that endogenously expressed acetylation-mimic TDP-43K145Q alters TDP-43 localization and conformation in response to stress and impairs splicing in a disease-relevant manner in human iPSC-derived neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing altered TDP-43 behavior in hiPSC-derived neurons.

claim: Endogenously expressed acetylation-mimic TDP-43K145Q alters TDP-43 conformation in response to stress in human iPSC-derived neurons.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that endogenously expressed acetylation-mimic TDP-43K145Q alters TDP-43 localization and conformation in response to stress and impairs splicing in a disease-relevant manner in human iPSC-derived neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing altered TDP-43 behavior in hiPSC-derived neurons.

claim: Endogenously expressed acetylation-mimic TDP-43K145Q impairs splicing in a disease-relevant manner in human iPSC-derived neurons.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that endogenously expressed acetylation-mimic TDP-43K145Q alters TDP-43 localization and conformation in response to stress and impairs splicing in a disease-relevant manner in human iPSC-derived neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing altered splicing in hiPSC-derived neurons.

claim: At 12 months old, TDP-43KQ/KQ mice showed significant reduction of body weight compared to WT littermates.
source: At 12 months old, TDP-43KQ/KQ mice showed significant reduction of body weight compared to WT littermates, and this difference was maintained until end point analysis at 18 months old (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The body weight difference between TDP-43KQ/KQ mice and WT littermates was maintained until end point analysis at 18 months old.
source: At 12 months old, TDP-43KQ/KQ mice showed significant reduction of body weight compared to WT littermates, and this difference was maintained until end point analysis at 18 months old (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TDP-43KQ/KQ mice spend significantly more time in the center region of an open-field test.
source: Evaluation of exploratory activity and locomotion in an open-field test demonstrated that TDP-43KQ/KQ mice spend significantly more time in the center region (Figure 4B), with no differences in total distance traveled (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), indicative of decreased anxiety-like behavior (Carola et al., 2002; Seibenhener and Wooten, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by open-field test data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There were no differences in total distance traveled in an open-field test between TDP-43KQ/KQ mice and WT littermates.
source: Evaluation of exploratory activity and locomotion in an open-field test demonstrated that TDP-43KQ/KQ mice spend significantly more time in the center region (Figure 4B), with no differences in total distance traveled (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), indicative of decreased anxiety-like behavior (Carola et al., 2002; Seibenhener and Wooten, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by open-field test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Spending more time in the center region of an open-field test is indicative of decreased anxiety-like behavior.
source: Evaluation of exploratory activity and locomotion in an open-field test demonstrated that TDP-43KQ/KQ mice spend significantly more time in the center region (Figure 4B), with no differences in total distance traveled (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), indicative of decreased anxiety-like behavior (Carola et al., 2002; Seibenhener and Wooten, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work on behavioral testing.

claim: Acoustic startle testing revealed impaired prepulse inhibition (PPI) in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 12 months old.
source: Acoustic startle testing revealed impaired prepulse inhibition (PPI) in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 12 months old (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), indicative of deficits in sensorimotor gating, a form of inhibitory behavioral control (Gómez-Nieto et al., 2020; Mena et al., 2016), which is a phenomenon that can be observed in early dementia (Ueki et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by acoustic startle test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Impaired prepulse inhibition is indicative of deficits in sensorimotor gating, a form of inhibitory behavioral control.
source: Acoustic startle testing revealed impaired prepulse inhibition (PPI) in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 12 months old (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), indicative of deficits in sensorimotor gating, a form of inhibitory behavioral control (Gómez-Nieto et al., 2020; Mena et al., 2016), which is a phenomenon that can be observed in early dementia (Ueki et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work on behavioral testing.

claim: Impaired prepulse inhibition is a phenomenon that can be observed in early dementia.
source: Acoustic startle testing revealed impaired prepulse inhibition (PPI) in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 12 months old (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), indicative of deficits in sensorimotor gating, a form of inhibitory behavioral control (Gómez-Nieto et al., 2020; Mena et al., 2016), which is a phenomenon that can be observed in early dementia (Ueki et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Context-dependent fear testing revealed reduced freezing times in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice, with trends observed at 12 months old and significant deficits appearing at 18 months.
source: Context-dependent fear testing revealed reduced freezing times in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice, with trends observed at 12 months old and significant deficits appearing at 18 months (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fear conditioning test data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Auditory cue-dependent fear testing revealed significant impairments in associative cue learning in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 12 months of age.
source: Similarly, auditory cue-dependent fear testing revealed significant impairments in associative cue learning in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 12 months of age (Figure 4D), a behavior thought to be mediated by the amygdala and higher-order cortical regions important in inhibitory control (Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by fear conditioning test data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Associative cue learning is a behavior thought to be mediated by the amygdala and higher-order cortical regions important in inhibitory control.
source: Similarly, auditory cue-dependent fear testing revealed significant impairments in associative cue learning in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 12 months of age (Figure 4D), a behavior thought to be mediated by the amygdala and higher-order cortical regions important in inhibitory control (Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work on behavioral neuroscience.

claim: Morris Water Maze testing showed equivalent swim speeds between TDP-43KQ/KQ mice and WT littermates, suggesting no motor impairments in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 18 months of age.
source: Morris Water Maze testing was used to evaluate swimming ability and spatial learning (Vorhees and Williams, 2006), which showed equivalent swim speeds, suggesting no motor impairments in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 18 months of age (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Morris Water Maze test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Assessment of spatial learning showed a trend toward impaired acquisition learning in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
source: While assessment of spatial learning showed a trend toward impaired acquisition learning (Figure 4E, F), we observed more prominent defects in reversal learning after moving the location of the platform, as determined by significant delays in escape latency.
evidence: This claim is supported by Morris Water Maze test data shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: TDP-43KQ/KQ mice showed more prominent defects in reversal learning after moving the location of the platform, as determined by significant delays in escape latency.
source: While assessment of spatial learning showed a trend toward impaired acquisition learning (Figure 4E, F), we observed more prominent defects in reversal learning after moving the location of the platform, as determined by significant delays in escape latency.
evidence: This claim is supported by Morris Water Maze test data.

claim: The findings support deficits in cognitive flexibility in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
source: Our findings support deficits in cognitive flexibility in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice (Figure 4G, H; Nicholls et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Morris Water Maze reversal learning data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: There were no overt signs of motor impairment in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 18 months of age.
source: To determine any ALS-like motor phenotypes, we assessed motor function and were surprised to find no overt signs of motor impairment in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 18 months of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by motor function testing data.

claim: TDP-43KQ/KQ mice performed similarly to WT littermates as assessed by rotarod testing.
source: TDP-43KQ/KQ mice performed similarly to WT littermates as assessed by rotarod testing (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C, D) and in grip strength as measured using digital force meters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by rotarod test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C and 3D.

claim: TDP-43KQ/KQ mice performed similarly to WT littermates in grip strength as measured using digital force meters.
source: TDP-43KQ/KQ mice performed similarly to WT littermates as assessed by rotarod testing (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C, D) and in grip strength as measured using digital force meters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: There were no differences in swim speed or distance traveled in an open field at any age tested between TDP-43KQ/KQ mice and WT littermates.
source: Moreover, there were no differences in swim speed or distance traveled in an open field at any age tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: The preferential deficits in learning and behavioral control support an age-dependent FTLD- or dementia-like phenotype in acetylation-mimic TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
source: The preferential deficits in learning and behavioral control support an age-dependent FTLD- or dementia-like phenotype in acetylation-mimic TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of behavioral deficits observed in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.

claim: No evidence of neuron loss was observed in the neocortex of TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 12 or 18 months of age.
source: We did not observe any evidence of neuron loss in the neocortex of TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at 12 or 18 months of age (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantitative image analysis data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: No astrogliosis was observed in the neocortex or hippocampus of TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
source: Similarly, we observed no astrogliosis (GFAP intensity and area occupied by GFAP+ cells) or microgliosis (Iba1 intensity and area occupied by Iba1+ cells) in the neocortex or hippocampus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No microgliosis was observed in the neocortex or hippocampus of TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
source: Similarly, we observed no astrogliosis (GFAP intensity and area occupied by GFAP+ cells) or microgliosis (Iba1 intensity and area occupied by Iba1+ cells) in the neocortex or hippocampus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Confocal microscopy and automated quantitative image analysis did not reveal nuclear or cytoplasmic TDP-43-positive inclusions in any brain region or genotype.
source: We initially used confocal microscopy, and automated quantitative image analysis to assess TDP-43 morphology and localization in the neocortex and hippocampus, which did not reveal nuclear or cytoplasmic TDP-43-positive inclusions in any brain region or genotype (Figure 5D, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5D and 5G.

claim: TDP-43KQ/KQ mouse neocortex harbored insoluble phosphorylated TDP-43 at the disease-associated Ser409/410 locus (p409/410) at 12 months of age.
source: TDP-43KQ/KQ mouse neocortex harbored insoluble phosphorylated TDP-43 at the disease-associated Ser409/410 locus (Neumann et al., 2009) (p409/410) at 12 months of age, which was even more prominent at 18 months (Figure 6A, C), a timepoint at which TDP-43KQ/KQ mice showed behavioral and cognitive defects (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A and 6C.

claim: Insoluble phosphorylated TDP-43 at p409/410 was even more prominent at 18 months in TDP-43KQ/KQ mouse neocortex.
source: TDP-43KQ/KQ mouse neocortex harbored insoluble phosphorylated TDP-43 at the disease-associated Ser409/410 locus (Neumann et al., 2009) (p409/410) at 12 months of age, which was even more prominent at 18 months (Figure 6A, C), a timepoint at which TDP-43KQ/KQ mice showed behavioral and cognitive defects (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A and 6C.

claim: p409/410 abundance was minimal in the hippocampus of 12-month-old TDP-43KQ/KQ mice but increased by 18 months.
source: Notably, p409/410 abundance was minimal in the hippocampus of 12-month-old TDP-43KQ/KQ mice but increased by 18 months (Figure 6D, F), coinciding with the onset of hippocampal-mediated learning deficits (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6D and 6F.

claim: The increase in p409/410 in the hippocampus coincided with the onset of hippocampal-mediated learning deficits.
source: Notably, p409/410 abundance was minimal in the hippocampus of 12-month-old TDP-43KQ/KQ mice but increased by 18 months (Figure 6D, F), coinciding with the onset of hippocampal-mediated learning deficits (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between biochemical changes and behavioral deficits.

claim: The total insoluble TDP-43 pool was not altered in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
source: Though p409/410 was elevated in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice, we were surprised to find that the total insoluble TDP-43 pool was not altered, suggesting that increased TDP-43 phosphorylation may precede overt conversion from soluble to insoluble TDP-43.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data.

claim: Increased TDP-43 phosphorylation may precede overt conversion from soluble to insoluble TDP-43.
source: Though p409/410 was elevated in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice, we were surprised to find that the total insoluble TDP-43 pool was not altered, suggesting that increased TDP-43 phosphorylation may precede overt conversion from soluble to insoluble TDP-43.
evidence: This claim is speculated based on the observation that phosphorylated TDP-43 increases without a corresponding increase in total insoluble TDP-43.

claim: The soluble TDP-43 pool was significantly increased in TDP-43KQ/KQ at 12 months in the neocortex.
source: The soluble TDP-43 pool was significantly increased in TDP-43KQ/KQ at 12 months in the neocortex and at 18 months in both neocortex (Figure 6A, B) and hippocampus (Figure 6D, E), an indicator of autoregulated TDP-43 protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The soluble TDP-43 pool was significantly increased in TDP-43KQ/KQ at 18 months in both neocortex and hippocampus.
source: The soluble TDP-43 pool was significantly increased in TDP-43KQ/KQ at 12 months in the neocortex and at 18 months in both neocortex (Figure 6A, B) and hippocampus (Figure 6D, E), an indicator of autoregulated TDP-43 protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A, 6B, 6D, and 6E.

claim: Increased soluble TDP-43 is an indicator of autoregulated TDP-43 protein levels.
source: The soluble TDP-43 pool was significantly increased in TDP-43KQ/KQ at 12 months in the neocortex and at 18 months in both neocortex (Figure 6A, B) and hippocampus (Figure 6D, E), an indicator of autoregulated TDP-43 protein levels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known autoregulatory mechanism of TDP-43.

claim: There was a striking increase in cytoplasmic TDP-43 in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at both 12 and 18 months of age in the neocortex and hippocampus.
source: To assess TDP-43 mislocalization using a biochemical approach, we performed subcellular fractionation to isolate nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins from the neocortex and hippocampus and found a striking increase in cytoplasmic TDP-43 in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at both 12 and 18 months of age (Figure 6G–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by subcellular fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 6G-L.

claim: TDP-43KQ/KQ mice harbored insoluble p(409/410)-TDP-43 in the spinal cord at 18 months old.
source: Surprisingly, TDP-43KQ/KQ mice harbored insoluble p(409/410)-TDP-43 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, C) and moderate increases in cytoplasmic TDP-43 mislocalization (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D–F) in the spinal cord at 18 months old, despite the lack of any overt motor deficits in TDP-43KQ/KQ animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and 3C.

claim: TDP-43KQ/KQ mice showed moderate increases in cytoplasmic TDP-43 mislocalization in the spinal cord at 18 months old.
source: Surprisingly, TDP-43KQ/KQ mice harbored insoluble p(409/410)-TDP-43 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, C) and moderate increases in cytoplasmic TDP-43 mislocalization (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D–F) in the spinal cord at 18 months old, despite the lack of any overt motor deficits in TDP-43KQ/KQ animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by subcellular fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D-F.

claim: A similar biochemical signature of TDP-43 abnormalities is present in the spinal cord, yet does not correlate with motor deficits in 12- to 18-month-old mice.
source: We thus found that a similar biochemical signature of TDP-43 abnormalities is present in the spinal cord, yet does not correlate with motor deficits in 12- to 18-month-old mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that spinal cord TDP-43 pathology does not correlate with motor deficits.

claim: TDP-43 phosphorylation and mislocalization occur as early events, prior to the formation of mature TDP-43 inclusion pathology.
source: Our findings suggest TDP-43 phosphorylation and mislocalization occur as early events, prior to the formation of mature TDP-43 inclusion pathology and may drive the progressive FTLD-TDP-like phenotype in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal pattern of TDP-43 pathology observed in the study.

claim: TDP-43 phosphorylation and mislocalization may drive the progressive FTLD-TDP-like phenotype in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
source: Our findings suggest TDP-43 phosphorylation and mislocalization occur as early events, prior to the formation of mature TDP-43 inclusion pathology and may drive the progressive FTLD-TDP-like phenotype in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
evidence: This claim is speculated based on the correlation between TDP-43 pathology and behavioral deficits.

claim: Nearly 400 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified in each brain region in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice compared to TDP-43wt.
source: We examined the neocortex and hippocampus of 18-month-old TDP-43wt or TDP-43KQ/KQ mice, representing the regions and timepoints with the most striking biochemical and behavioral and abnormalities and identified nearly 400 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in each brain region in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice compared to TDP-43wt, after correcting for underlying batch effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: The Tardbp transcript was increased in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
source: As expected by acetylation-induced loss of TDP-43 function and subsequent autoregulation, the Tardbp transcript was increased (Supplementary file 1a, b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Follow-up RT-qPCR analysis confirmed a two- to threefold increase in Tardbp expression in the neocortex and hippocampus.
source: Follow-up RT-qPCR analysis confirmed a two- to threefold increase in Tardbp expression in the neocortex and hippocampus (Figure 6M, N), as well as the spinal cord (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which correlated with increased TDP-43 protein levels (Figure 6B, E; Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6M and 6N.

claim: Follow-up RT-qPCR analysis confirmed a two- to threefold increase in Tardbp expression in the spinal cord.
source: Follow-up RT-qPCR analysis confirmed a two- to threefold increase in Tardbp expression in the neocortex and hippocampus (Figure 6M, N), as well as the spinal cord (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which correlated with increased TDP-43 protein levels (Figure 6B, E; Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Increased Tardbp expression correlated with increased TDP-43 protein levels.
source: Follow-up RT-qPCR analysis confirmed a two- to threefold increase in Tardbp expression in the neocortex and hippocampus (Figure 6M, N), as well as the spinal cord (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which correlated with increased TDP-43 protein levels (Figure 6B, E; Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between mRNA and protein levels.

claim: The most highly downregulated genes in both brain regions were involved in developmental processes, including many related to CNS development and maintenance.
source: In both brain regions, the most highly downregulated genes were involved in developmental processes, including many related to CNS development and maintenance, such as neurogenesis (e.g., Sema5b, Rnd2, Brinp1), gliogenesis (e.g., Tlr2, Olig2, Sox10), and myelination (e.g., Nkx2-2, Nkx6-2, Sox10).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Sema5b was the most dramatically reduced transcript in the hippocampus.
source: Sema5b was the most dramatically reduced transcript in the hippocampus, and the third most highly reduced in the cortex (Supplementary file 1a, b) with a twofold reduction in expression in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Sema5b was the third most highly reduced transcript in the cortex.
source: Sema5b was the most dramatically reduced transcript in the hippocampus, and the third most highly reduced in the cortex (Supplementary file 1a, b) with a twofold reduction in expression in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Sema5b showed a twofold reduction in expression in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
source: Sema5b was the most dramatically reduced transcript in the hippocampus, and the third most highly reduced in the cortex (Supplementary file 1a, b) with a twofold reduction in expression in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Genes related to GABAergic synapses were selectively downregulated in the neocortex.
source: Genes related to GABAergic synapses (e.g., Gad1, Gad2, Abat, Gnb5) were selectively downregulated in the neocortex, while trans-synaptic signaling and ion transport mechanisms (e.g., Homer3, Camk4a, Nsmf, Cnih2) were decreased in the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Trans-synaptic signaling and ion transport mechanisms were decreased in the hippocampus.
source: Genes related to GABAergic synapses (e.g., Gad1, Gad2, Abat, Gnb5) were selectively downregulated in the neocortex, while trans-synaptic signaling and ion transport mechanisms (e.g., Homer3, Camk4a, Nsmf, Cnih2) were decreased in the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: There was significant upregulation of cellular stress response genes in both the hippocampus and neocortex.
source: In contrast, there was significant upregulation of cellular stress response genes (Sesn1, Nrros, Plat, Klf15) and many apoptotic regulators (e.g., Trp53inp1, Pmaip1, Bcl2l1, Plekhf1) in both the hippocampus and neocortex, along with an over-representation of GO terms related to metabolism, localization, and cell adhesion (Figure 7, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7.

claim: There was significant upregulation of many apoptotic regulators in both the hippocampus and neocortex.
source: In contrast, there was significant upregulation of cellular stress response genes (Sesn1, Nrros, Plat, Klf15) and many apoptotic regulators (e.g., Trp53inp1, Pmaip1, Bcl2l1, Plekhf1) in both the hippocampus and neocortex, along with an over-representation of GO terms related to metabolism, localization, and cell adhesion (Figure 7, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Coagulation and complement cascades were only upregulated in the hippocampus.
source: Several pathways were uniquely altered including coagulation and complement cascades, which were only upregulated in the hippocampus (e.g., F3, Plat, Cd59a).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Comparison of the DEGs in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice to the mouse orthologs of those found in FTLD-TDP frontal or temporal cortex tissue revealed marked overlap between the mouse and human datasets.
source: Comparison of the DEGs in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice to the mouse orthologs of those found in FTLD-TDP frontal or temporal cortex tissue (Hasan et al., 2022) revealed marked overlap between our mouse and their human datasets (Figure 7, see 'FTLD-TDP Cortex' bar), particularly in the hippocampus, as measured by statistical enrichment analyses that found over-representation of FTLD-TDP DEGs in our TDP-43KQ/KQ dataset (Supplementary file 1d; p = 0.0003 'Hippocampus Down' vs Downregulated in FTLD-TDP frontal cortex; p = 0.0014 'Hippocampus Down' vs Downregulated in FTLD-TDP temporal cortex; p = 0.0048 'Hippocampus Up' vs Upregulated in FTLD-TDP frontal cortex).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNA sequencing data to published human FTLD-TDP data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Analysis of TDP-43KQ/KQ neocortex identified 289 differentially spliced genes (DSGs), with 81.7% of loci containing at least one cryptic splice junction.
source: Analysis of TDP-43KQ/KQ neocortex identified 289 differentially spliced genes (DSGs), with 81.7% of loci containing at least one cryptic splice junction, and 29.8% containing two cryptic splice junctions (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing and splicing analysis data.

claim: In the hippocampus, 126 DSGs were found, 77.0% of which contain a cryptic splice junction and 41.3% that are formed by two cryptic splice sites.
source: In the hippocampus, we found 126 DSGs, 77.0% of which contain a cryptic splice junction and 41.3% that are formed by two cryptic splice sites (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing and splicing analysis data.

claim: Over 70% of the DSGs identified in the hippocampus were also present in the cortex.
source: The alternative splicing events were relatively consistent between brain regions, as over 70% of the DSGs identified in the hippocampus were also present in the cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing and splicing analysis data.

claim: Among the most significant DSGs identified were known TDP-43 splicing targets (e.g., Kcnip2, Pdp1, Poldipp3, Ppfibp1, Dnajc5, Tmem2, Sort1).
source: Among the most significant DSGs identified were known TDP-43 splicing targets (e.g., Kcnip2, Pdp1, Poldipp3, Ppfibp1, Dnajc5, Tmem2, Sort1) (Fratta et al., 2018; Arnold et al., 2013; Polymenidou et al., 2011), transcripts associated with particular neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., Mapt, Atxn1, Lrrk2) (Trabzuni et al., 2012; Park et al., 2016; Giesert et al., 2013; Lacognata et al., 2015; Rosas et al., 2020; Manek et al., 2020; Banfi et al., 1994), and also many robustly altered transcripts that are poorly characterized but linked to neurodegeneration (e.g., Nrxn3, Nos1, Arfgef2, Arhgap10, Lrp8, Smarca4, Rims2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing and splicing analysis data, with citations to prior work.

claim: Sort1 was the most substantially altered transcript among all identified DSGs.
source: Of all identified DSGs, the most substantially altered transcript was Sort1, encoding the Sortilin-1 (Sort1) protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing and splicing analysis data.

claim: Exclusion of a Sort1 3′ exon was reduced by 55.9% in TDP-43KQ/KQ cortex.
source: We noticed that exclusion of a Sort1 3′ exon was reduced by 55.9% in TDP-43KQ/KQ cortex and by 57.0% in the hippocampus (Figure 8A), such that the aberrantly spliced Sort1 transcript was the predominant variant detected, comprising nearly 80% of all Sort1 transcripts, aligning with our findings from TDP-43KQ/KQ primary mouse cortical neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing and splicing analysis data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Exclusion of a Sort1 3′ exon was reduced by 57.0% in TDP-43KQ/KQ hippocampus.
source: We noticed that exclusion of a Sort1 3′ exon was reduced by 55.9% in TDP-43KQ/KQ cortex and by 57.0% in the hippocampus (Figure 8A), such that the aberrantly spliced Sort1 transcript was the predominant variant detected, comprising nearly 80% of all Sort1 transcripts, aligning with our findings from TDP-43KQ/KQ primary mouse cortical neurons.

claim: The ratio of aberrant Sort1-ex17b to appropriately spliced Sort1-WT was increased approximately 10-fold in the neocortex of TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at both 12 and 18 months of age.
source: We found the ratio of aberrant Sort1-ex17b to appropriately spliced Sort1-WT was increased approximately 10-fold in the neocortex (Figure 8B) and hippocampus (Figure 8C) of TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at both 12 and 18 months of age, which corroborates our RNA sequencing analysis showing that the exon-included Sort1+ex17b variant predominates in these tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The ratio of aberrant Sort1-ex17b to appropriately spliced Sort1-WT was increased approximately 10-fold in the hippocampus of TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at both 12 and 18 months of age.
source: We found the ratio of aberrant Sort1-ex17b to appropriately spliced Sort1-WT was increased approximately 10-fold in the neocortex (Figure 8B) and hippocampus (Figure 8C) of TDP-43KQ/KQ mice at both 12 and 18 months of age, which corroborates our RNA sequencing analysis showing that the exon-included Sort1+ex17b variant predominates in these tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: A higher molecular weight Sort1 variant was identified in TDP-43KQ/KQ compared to WT mice, consistent with Sort1 exon 17b inclusion.
source: To determine whether the Sort1+ex17b transcript in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice leads to the generation of a distinct Sort1 protein product, we immunoblotted hippocampus and cortex homogenates and identified a higher molecular weight Sort1 variant in TDP-43KQ/KQ compared to WT mice (Figure 8D, E), consistent with Sort1 exon 17b inclusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8D and 8E.

claim: The abnormal Sort1 protein showed decreased steady-state stability in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice, as suggested by reduced protein levels in acetylation-mimic animals, compared to controls.
source: The abnormal Sort1 protein showed decreased steady-state stability in TDP-43KQ/KQ mice, as suggested by reduced protein levels in acetylation-mimic animals, compared to controls (Figure 8F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8F and 8G.

claim: Disrupting RNA binding with an acetylation-mimic TDP-43K145Q mutation results in an age-dependent, dementia-like phenotype characterized by signatures of FTLD.
source: In conclusion, disrupting RNA binding with an acetylation-mimic TDP-43K145Q mutation results in an age-dependent, dementia-like phenotype characterized by signatures of FTLD, including progressive cognitive deficits, TDP-43 mislocalization and phosphorylation, impaired autoregulation, and prominent RNA dysregulation.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: TDP-43 acetylation affected many known FTLD-associated pathways, including STMN2, SORT1, and stress response signaling.
source: TDP-43 acetylation affected many known FTLD-associated pathways, including STMN2, SORT1, and stress response signaling, while also pinpointing new putative pathways as mediators of disease pathogenesis.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: By developing models of TDP-43 acetylation, we expand our understanding of sporadic TDP-43 proteinopathies.
source: By developing models of TDP-43 acetylation, we expand our understanding of sporadic TDP-43 proteinopathies and provide new avenues to identify therapeutics that target the pathogenic mechanisms underlying TDP-43 proteinopathies.
evidence: This claim is a statement about the significance of the study.
